items.title: I can explain the purpose of a logbook in a scientific investigation
items.what: A logbook is a dated, handwritten record of all stages of an investigation — from planning through to results and reflections. It authenticates primary data by showing it was recorded firsthand by the investigator.
items.why: VCE requires students to maintain a logbook for all practical activities in Units 1–4. A physical logbook reduces the likelihood of tampering with results and provides verifiable evidence of authentic data collection.
items.example: A student records the date, the title of their investigation, their aim, hypothesis, method and results table all in their logbook before conducting the experiment. Each entry is dated so the sequence of work can be verified.

subtopic.name: Investigative Planning and Design
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to structure and document a scientific investigation using a logbook. It includes how to write each section of the logbook — from the title and introduction through to the method — and what level of detail is required for each.
subtopic.why: A well-kept logbook is required for VCE assessment and authenticates that primary data was collected by the investigator. Clear documentation also allows others to repeat or reproduce your investigation, which is essential for valid scientific practice.

items.title: I can write a clear and specific title for a scientific investigation
items.what: A title states the research question under investigation and should reference both the independent variable (what is being changed) and the dependent variable (what is being measured).
items.why: A specific title immediately communicates the scope of the investigation to any reader and distinguishes a focused, single-variable exploration from a vague or overly broad question.
items.example: A weak title: 'Determine the effect of a catalyst on the rate of a chemical reaction.' A stronger title: 'Does the addition of invertase result in an increased rate of glucose production through its function as a catalyst on the hydrolysis of sucrose?'

subtopic.name: Investigative Planning and Design
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to structure and document a scientific investigation using a logbook. It includes how to write each section of the logbook — from the title and introduction through to the method — and what level of detail is required for each.
subtopic.why: A well-kept logbook is required for VCE assessment and authenticates that primary data was collected by the investigator. Clear documentation also allows others to repeat or reproduce your investigation, which is essential for valid scientific practice.

items.title: I can write an introduction that explains the chemical context of an investigation
items.what: The introduction provides a detailed but concise explanation of the chemistry behind the investigation. It includes relevant chemical equations, key concepts and definitions, and links the background theory to the aim and hypothesis.
items.why: Examiners assess whether students understand the chemistry underpinning their investigation, not just the procedure. A strong introduction demonstrates that the experimental design is grounded in scientific theory.
items.example: In an invertase investigation, the introduction would explain that invertase is an enzyme that catalyses the hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose, lowering activation energy. It would include the equation: C12H22O11(aq) + H2O(l) → C6H12O6(aq) + C6H12O6(aq).

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to structure and document a scientific investigation using a logbook. It includes how to write each section of the logbook — from the title and introduction through to the method — and what level of detail is required for each.
subtopic.why: A well-kept logbook is required for VCE assessment and authenticates that primary data was collected by the investigator. Clear documentation also allows others to repeat or reproduce your investigation, which is essential for valid scientific practice.

items.title: I can write a method with sufficient detail for the investigation to be repeated
items.what: A method is a series of clearly numbered steps that describes exactly how the investigation was conducted, including specific quantities, concentrations, equipment, timepoints and any control conditions.
items.why: A method that lacks specific quantities or equipment cannot be repeated by other investigators, which means the investigation cannot be confirmed as reproducible. VCE assessment requires methods detailed enough for full reproducibility.
items.example: A weak method step: 'Add enzyme to the test tube.' A stronger step: 'Add 3.00 mL of 5.0 x 10^-2 mg mL^-1 invertase solution to the test tube containing 3.00 mL of 50.0 mg mL^-1 sucrose solution pre-incubated at 40.0°C.'

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to structure and document a scientific investigation using a logbook. It includes how to write each section of the logbook — from the title and introduction through to the method — and what level of detail is required for each.
subtopic.why: A well-kept logbook is required for VCE assessment and authenticates that primary data was collected by the investigator. Clear documentation also allows others to repeat or reproduce your investigation, which is essential for valid scientific practice.

items.title: I can distinguish between primary data and secondary data
items.what: Primary data is collected firsthand by the investigator through experiments, observations, fieldwork or surveys. Secondary data is existing data collected by someone else, such as published journal articles, books or websites.
items.why: Understanding this distinction matters for logbook authentication and for correctly citing sources. VCE investigations require students to generate their own primary data, but the introduction often draws on secondary sources to establish context.
items.example: The glucose concentration readings a student records from their own titration experiment are primary data. The accepted value for the specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J g^-1 °C^-1) found in a textbook is secondary data.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to structure and document a scientific investigation using a logbook. It includes how to write each section of the logbook — from the title and introduction through to the method — and what level of detail is required for each.
subtopic.why: A well-kept logbook is required for VCE assessment and authenticates that primary data was collected by the investigator. Clear documentation also allows others to repeat or reproduce your investigation, which is essential for valid scientific practice.

items.title: I can define and identify the independent variable in an experiment
items.what: The independent variable is the variable that the experimenter deliberately changes. In a single-variable exploration, there is only one independent variable, and all specific values tested should be listed.
items.why: Clearly identifying the independent variable ensures the investigation has a defined focus. It also helps the experimenter design a method where only one thing changes at a time, which is necessary for drawing valid conclusions.
items.example: In an investigation into how concentration of HCl affects the rate of neutralisation with NaOH, the independent variable is the concentration of the HCl and NaOH solutions. The values tested are 0.10 M, 0.50 M, 1.0 M and 2.0 M.

subtopic.name: Variables, Controls and Validity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the identification and correct use of independent, dependent and controlled variables. It also explains what makes an investigation a controlled experiment and a single-variable exploration, and how these features relate to validity.
subtopic.why: Correctly identifying and controlling variables is the foundation of a valid experiment. If variables are not controlled, it is impossible to determine whether the independent variable caused the observed changes in the dependent variable.

items.title: I can define and identify the dependent variable in an experiment
items.what: The dependent variable is the variable that changes in response to the independent variable. It is what the experimenter measures, and the method of measurement (instrument and units) should be stated.
items.why: Specifying how the dependent variable will be measured is essential for precision and reproducibility. It also determines what type of data is collected and how results will be represented.
items.example: In the HCl and NaOH neutralisation experiment, the dependent variable is the change in temperature of the combined solution, measured in degrees Celsius (°C) using a thermometer after one minute.

subtopic.name: Variables, Controls and Validity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the identification and correct use of independent, dependent and controlled variables. It also explains what makes an investigation a controlled experiment and a single-variable exploration, and how these features relate to validity.
subtopic.why: Correctly identifying and controlling variables is the foundation of a valid experiment. If variables are not controlled, it is impossible to determine whether the independent variable caused the observed changes in the dependent variable.

items.title: I can identify and list controlled variables in an experiment
items.what: Controlled variables are all the factors that are kept constant throughout the experiment so they do not influence the dependent variable. There is always more than one controlled variable, and the word 'same' is used to describe each.
items.why: If controlled variables are allowed to change, it becomes impossible to determine whether the independent variable caused any observed change. Listing controlled variables demonstrates awareness of what could introduce error if not managed.
items.example: In an invertase investigation, controlled variables include: same initial concentration of sucrose (50.0 mg mL^-1), same volume of solutions added (3.00 mL each), same temperature of all solutions (40.0°C), and same equipment used throughout.

subtopic.name: Variables, Controls and Validity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the identification and correct use of independent, dependent and controlled variables. It also explains what makes an investigation a controlled experiment and a single-variable exploration, and how these features relate to validity.
subtopic.why: Correctly identifying and controlling variables is the foundation of a valid experiment. If variables are not controlled, it is impossible to determine whether the independent variable caused the observed changes in the dependent variable.

items.title: I can define a controlled experiment and list its key features
items.what: A controlled experiment is one that includes a control group (tested under normal conditions without the experimental variable) alongside experimental groups. It has one independent variable, one dependent variable, and all other variables kept constant.
items.why: A controlled experiment allows results from experimental conditions to be compared against a baseline. Without a control group, it is difficult to determine whether any observed change was caused by the independent variable.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, the control group is the test tube with sucrose and distilled water (no enzyme added). This is compared against the experimental group, which has sucrose and invertase added, allowing any difference in glucose concentration to be attributed to the enzyme.

subtopic.name: Variables, Controls and Validity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the identification and correct use of independent, dependent and controlled variables. It also explains what makes an investigation a controlled experiment and a single-variable exploration, and how these features relate to validity.
subtopic.why: Correctly identifying and controlling variables is the foundation of a valid experiment. If variables are not controlled, it is impossible to determine whether the independent variable caused the observed changes in the dependent variable.

items.title: I can explain what single-variable exploration means and why it matters
items.what: A single-variable exploration is an investigation that contains only one independent variable and one dependent variable. All other variables are controlled so that any change in the dependent variable can be attributed solely to the independent variable.
items.why: Without single-variable exploration, conclusions from an investigation are not valid. If two variables change simultaneously, it is impossible to know which one caused the observed effect.
items.example: A research question asking 'How do temperature and concentration affect the potential difference of galvanic cells?' is not a single-variable exploration because it has two independent variables. It would need to be split into two separate investigations.

subtopic.name: Variables, Controls and Validity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the identification and correct use of independent, dependent and controlled variables. It also explains what makes an investigation a controlled experiment and a single-variable exploration, and how these features relate to validity.
subtopic.why: Correctly identifying and controlling variables is the foundation of a valid experiment. If variables are not controlled, it is impossible to determine whether the independent variable caused the observed changes in the dependent variable.

items.title: I can define validity and explain how to design a valid investigation
items.what: Validity refers to the extent to which all variables in an experiment have been controlled so that the independent variable is the only factor that changes. A valid experiment can produce results that are attributable to the independent variable alone.
items.why: An investigation that is not valid cannot support or refute a hypothesis with confidence. Validity is a prerequisite for drawing meaningful scientific conclusions.
items.example: In the invertase investigation, validity is achieved by keeping the volume of sucrose (3.00 mL), concentration of sucrose (50.0 mg mL^-1), temperature (40.0°C) and volume of invertase (3.00 mL) all constant across all trials.

subtopic.name: Variables, Controls and Validity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the identification and correct use of independent, dependent and controlled variables. It also explains what makes an investigation a controlled experiment and a single-variable exploration, and how these features relate to validity.
subtopic.why: Correctly identifying and controlling variables is the foundation of a valid experiment. If variables are not controlled, it is impossible to determine whether the independent variable caused the observed changes in the dependent variable.

items.title: I can distinguish between an aim and a hypothesis
items.what: An aim states the main purpose of an investigation — what it intends to find out. A hypothesis is a testable prediction of the expected outcome, based on existing theory, that can be supported or refuted by experimental results.
items.why: Confusing these two terms is a common error in VCE reports. An aim does not predict an outcome; a hypothesis does. Both are needed and serve different functions in structuring an investigation.
items.example: Aim: 'To determine whether the presence of the enzyme invertase increases the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose.' Hypothesis: 'The presence of invertase will increase the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose, producing a higher concentration of glucose, because invertase lowers the activation energy of the reaction.'

subtopic.name: Aims, Hypotheses and Ethics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to write well-formed aims and hypotheses, how to distinguish between them, and how to evaluate the health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to a practical investigation.
subtopic.why: Clear aims and hypotheses focus an investigation and allow results to be evaluated against predictions. Addressing safety and ethics is a VCE requirement and reflects responsible scientific practice.

items.title: I can write a specific aim that references the independent and dependent variables
items.what: A well-written aim explicitly names both the independent and dependent variables and uses precise language. It should be a single, clear statement of what the investigation intends to measure or determine.
items.why: A vague aim makes it difficult to design a focused method and to evaluate results against the purpose of the investigation. Explicit variable reference also helps ensure the investigation is a single-variable exploration.
items.example: Weak aim: 'To determine whether the presence of an enzyme increases the rate of a chemical reaction.' Stronger aim: 'To determine whether the presence of invertase increases the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose by measuring the concentration of glucose produced using glucose test strips.'

subtopic.name: Aims, Hypotheses and Ethics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to write well-formed aims and hypotheses, how to distinguish between them, and how to evaluate the health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to a practical investigation.
subtopic.why: Clear aims and hypotheses focus an investigation and allow results to be evaluated against predictions. Addressing safety and ethics is a VCE requirement and reflects responsible scientific practice.

items.title: I can write a hypothesis that is supported by scientific theory
items.what: A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction that states what will happen to the dependent variable when the independent variable is changed, with a scientific reason drawn from relevant theory.
items.why: A hypothesis grounded in theory demonstrates understanding of the chemistry involved. If results contradict the hypothesis, the theory provides a basis for evaluating whether the experimental design or the prediction needs revision.
items.example: Weak hypothesis: 'The enzyme will increase the rate of reaction.' Strong hypothesis: 'The presence of invertase will increase the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose, producing an increased concentration of glucose, because invertase catalyses the reaction by lowering its activation energy via an alternative reaction pathway.'

subtopic.name: Aims, Hypotheses and Ethics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to write well-formed aims and hypotheses, how to distinguish between them, and how to evaluate the health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to a practical investigation.
subtopic.why: Clear aims and hypotheses focus an investigation and allow results to be evaluated against predictions. Addressing safety and ethics is a VCE requirement and reflects responsible scientific practice.

items.title: I can define repeatability and reproducibility and distinguish between them
items.what: Repeatability is the ability to obtain the same results when the same experiment is repeated in the same laboratory by the same operator under the same conditions. Reproducibility is when the same results are obtained by different operators using different equipment.
items.why: These two terms are frequently confused in VCE responses. Repeatability improves reliability within one lab context; reproducibility strengthens scientific confidence by showing results hold across different conditions and investigators.
items.example: A student repeats the invertase experiment three times in their own lab — this tests repeatability. If another student in a different school runs the same experiment and gets similar results, that demonstrates reproducibility.

subtopic.name: Aims, Hypotheses and Ethics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to write well-formed aims and hypotheses, how to distinguish between them, and how to evaluate the health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to a practical investigation.
subtopic.why: Clear aims and hypotheses focus an investigation and allow results to be evaluated against predictions. Addressing safety and ethics is a VCE requirement and reflects responsible scientific practice.

items.title: I can identify health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to an investigation
items.what: Safety considerations include identifying hazardous substances and equipment, and specifying required personal protective equipment (PPE) such as lab coats, gloves and safety glasses. Ethical considerations address whether living organisms are used and how any potential harm is minimised or justified.
items.why: VCE investigations require explicit safety and ethics documentation. Failing to address these reduces the quality of a logbook entry and can also lead to unsafe laboratory practices.
items.example: For the invertase investigation: safety requires lab coat, gloves and safety glasses. For ethics: the invertase used was commercially manufactured yeast-derived enzyme, so no living plants or animals were harmed in obtaining it. This addresses the ethical consideration of using living organisms.

subtopic.name: Aims, Hypotheses and Ethics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to write well-formed aims and hypotheses, how to distinguish between them, and how to evaluate the health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to a practical investigation.
subtopic.why: Clear aims and hypotheses focus an investigation and allow results to be evaluated against predictions. Addressing safety and ethics is a VCE requirement and reflects responsible scientific practice.

items.title: I can identify sources of bias and explain how to minimise them
items.what: Bias occurs when aspects of the experimental design or data collection method consistently favour a particular outcome. Bias can be minimised by using blind measurement techniques, calibrating instruments against known standards, and ensuring controlled variables are truly constant.
items.why: Unaddressed bias compromises the validity and accuracy of results. Identifying and mitigating bias is a sign of a well-designed investigation and is rewarded in VCE extended response marking.
items.example: In the invertase glucose test strip experiment, bias could arise if the researcher subjectively interprets colour comparisons. Calibrating the test strips against a series of known glucose standard solutions before use would reduce this bias.

subtopic.name: Aims, Hypotheses and Ethics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to write well-formed aims and hypotheses, how to distinguish between them, and how to evaluate the health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to a practical investigation.
subtopic.why: Clear aims and hypotheses focus an investigation and allow results to be evaluated against predictions. Addressing safety and ethics is a VCE requirement and reflects responsible scientific practice.

items.title: I can distinguish between qualitative and quantitative data
items.what: Qualitative data is descriptive and expressed in words rather than numbers, such as colour, appearance or texture. Quantitative data is numerical, based on counting or measuring, and is expressed with appropriate units.
items.why: The type of data collected determines how it should be recorded and represented graphically. Misidentifying data type leads to incorrect graph choice and lost marks in VCE assessment tasks.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, observing that the glucose test strip 'turned dark brown' is qualitative data. Recording that the glucose concentration was 10.0 mg mL^-1 is quantitative data.

subtopic.name: Scientific Evidence and Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to collect, record and represent data appropriately. It includes the distinction between qualitative and quantitative data, the concept of resolution, how to construct correct results tables and graphs, and how to identify trends in data.
subtopic.why: Correctly organising and representing data is a core scientific skill assessed in VCE. Well-structured tables and graphs make it possible to identify patterns, support or refute hypotheses, and communicate findings clearly.

items.title: I can explain what resolution means and how it affects data recording
items.what: Resolution refers to the smallest change in a quantity that results in a noticeable change in the reading on a measuring instrument. The resolution of the instrument determines how many decimal places can be recorded.
items.why: Recording data to more decimal places than the instrument allows is scientifically dishonest and inaccurate. Recording to fewer decimal places than possible wastes the precision available from the instrument.
items.example: A gas syringe with markings every 1 mL has a resolution of 1.0 mL, allowing estimation to the nearest 0.1 mL (e.g. 11.3 mL). A burette with markings every 0.1 mL has a resolution of 0.1 mL, allowing estimation to 0.01 mL (e.g. 40.73 mL).

subtopic.name: Scientific Evidence and Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to collect, record and represent data appropriately. It includes the distinction between qualitative and quantitative data, the concept of resolution, how to construct correct results tables and graphs, and how to identify trends in data.
subtopic.why: Correctly organising and representing data is a core scientific skill assessed in VCE. Well-structured tables and graphs make it possible to identify patterns, support or refute hypotheses, and communicate findings clearly.

items.title: I can construct a correctly formatted results table
items.what: A results table must include a title referencing both variables, column headings with units, the independent variable in the first column, consistent decimal places across all values, results for all trials, and a calculated mean that excludes outliers.
items.why: An incorrectly formatted table is a common source of lost marks in VCE. Each convention — from decimal consistency to the placement of units in headings — reflects professional scientific recording practice.
items.example: Column heading 'Concentration of glucose (mg mL^-1)' is correct. Writing '10.0 mg mL^-1' inside a cell is incorrect — units belong in the heading only. All values in a column should be recorded to the same number of decimal places, e.g. 0.00, 1.00, 3.00, not 0, 1, 3.

subtopic.name: Scientific Evidence and Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to collect, record and represent data appropriately. It includes the distinction between qualitative and quantitative data, the concept of resolution, how to construct correct results tables and graphs, and how to identify trends in data.
subtopic.why: Correctly organising and representing data is a core scientific skill assessed in VCE. Well-structured tables and graphs make it possible to identify patterns, support or refute hypotheses, and communicate findings clearly.

items.title: I can choose the correct graph type to represent a given dataset
items.what: Continuous data (measured quantities such as time, temperature, concentration or volume) should be represented as a line graph with a line of best fit. Discrete data (countable, distinct categories) should be represented as a bar graph with gaps between bars.
items.why: Using a bar graph for continuous data, or a line graph for discrete data, is incorrect and reflects a misunderstanding of data types. VCE marking rubrics specifically assess correct graph type selection.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, glucose concentration measured over time (0 s, 60 s, 120 s, 180 s, 240 s, 300 s) is continuous data — a line graph is appropriate. If comparing the number of reactions that produced a precipitate across four different metal types, a bar graph would be appropriate.

subtopic.name: Scientific Evidence and Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to collect, record and represent data appropriately. It includes the distinction between qualitative and quantitative data, the concept of resolution, how to construct correct results tables and graphs, and how to identify trends in data.
subtopic.why: Correctly organising and representing data is a core scientific skill assessed in VCE. Well-structured tables and graphs make it possible to identify patterns, support or refute hypotheses, and communicate findings clearly.

items.title: I can construct a correctly labelled graph with a line of best fit
items.what: A graph must include a title, fully labelled axes with units, the independent variable on the x-axis, the dependent variable on the y-axis, evenly spaced axis scales, and a line of best fit that is drawn so the distances of points above and below the line are approximately equal.
items.why: A line of best fit shows the general trend and is used for making predictions. Common errors — such as connecting the dots rather than drawing a smooth trend line, or not starting scales at appropriate values — reduce the quality and interpretability of a graph.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, the x-axis is labelled 'Time (s)' with values 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, and the y-axis is 'Concentration of glucose produced (mg mL^-1)' with values 0 to 25. The line of best fit is smooth and does not need to pass through the first or last point.

subtopic.name: Scientific Evidence and Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to collect, record and represent data appropriately. It includes the distinction between qualitative and quantitative data, the concept of resolution, how to construct correct results tables and graphs, and how to identify trends in data.
subtopic.why: Correctly organising and representing data is a core scientific skill assessed in VCE. Well-structured tables and graphs make it possible to identify patterns, support or refute hypotheses, and communicate findings clearly.

items.title: I can identify and describe trends in experimental data
items.what: Identifying trends means describing the overall relationship between the independent and dependent variables, noting any changes in the gradient, and quoting specific data values from tables or graphs to support the description.
items.why: Trend identification is the basis of discussion and conclusion writing. Unsupported trend statements ('the results increased') without reference to data are insufficient for VCE extended response tasks.
items.example: In the invertase experiment: 'The concentration of glucose increased from 0.00 mg mL^-1 at 0 s to 20.0 mg mL^-1 at 180 s in the presence of invertase, after which it plateaued and remained constant at 20.0 mg mL^-1 through to 300 s.'

subtopic.name: Scientific Evidence and Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to collect, record and represent data appropriately. It includes the distinction between qualitative and quantitative data, the concept of resolution, how to construct correct results tables and graphs, and how to identify trends in data.
subtopic.why: Correctly organising and representing data is a core scientific skill assessed in VCE. Well-structured tables and graphs make it possible to identify patterns, support or refute hypotheses, and communicate findings clearly.

items.title: I can define accuracy and explain how it relates to the true value
items.what: Accuracy refers to how close the experimental measurements are to the true (accepted) value of the quantity being measured. An investigation may not always have a known true value for comparison, in which case accuracy cannot be fully determined.
items.why: Accuracy is often confused with precision in VCE responses. Understanding that accuracy depends on comparing results to an accepted standard — not to other trials — is a key distinction.
items.example: In the specific heat capacity investigation, the students' average result of 0.459 J g^-1 °C^-1 was very close to the accepted value for iron of 0.450 J g^-1 °C^-1, indicating high accuracy.

subtopic.name: Errors, Accuracy and Precision
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of experimental error — random and systematic — as well as the concepts of accuracy, precision, outliers and how to identify areas for improvement in investigation design.
subtopic.why: Understanding error analysis is essential for evaluating the quality of experimental results. VCE extended response tasks frequently require students to identify specific errors, explain their effect and propose improvements.

items.title: I can define precision and identify what affects it
items.what: Precision refers to how close repeated measurements are to each other, regardless of whether they are close to the true value. Precision is improved by using instruments with finer resolution and by repeating measurements.
items.why: Results can be precise but not accurate (consistently wrong in the same direction) or accurate but not precise (correct on average but widely spread). VCE requires students to distinguish and discuss these separately.
items.example: In the specific heat capacity investigation, the five trials (0.460, 0.455, 0.458, 0.460, 0.462 J g^-1 °C^-1) are very close together, indicating high precision. Replacing a colour-comparison glucose test strip with a digital glucometer would improve precision in the invertase experiment.

subtopic.name: Errors, Accuracy and Precision
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of experimental error — random and systematic — as well as the concepts of accuracy, precision, outliers and how to identify areas for improvement in investigation design.
subtopic.why: Understanding error analysis is essential for evaluating the quality of experimental results. VCE extended response tasks frequently require students to identify specific errors, explain their effect and propose improvements.

items.title: I can define systematic error and explain why it cannot be fixed by repeating measurements
items.what: A systematic error is when measurements consistently differ from the true value in the same direction every time — always too high or always too low. It results from a flaw in the method, equipment calibration or experimental design.
items.why: Because systematic errors affect all results equally, increasing the sample size or calculating a mean does not reduce them. The error can only be corrected by changing the method or recalibrating the equipment.
items.example: If a balance used to measure mass has not been tared (zeroed) before use, every mass reading will be too high by a consistent amount. This is a systematic error. Repeating the measurement does not fix it; recalibrating the balance does.

subtopic.name: Errors, Accuracy and Precision
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of experimental error — random and systematic — as well as the concepts of accuracy, precision, outliers and how to identify areas for improvement in investigation design.
subtopic.why: Understanding error analysis is essential for evaluating the quality of experimental results. VCE extended response tasks frequently require students to identify specific errors, explain their effect and propose improvements.

items.title: I can define random error and explain how repeating measurements reduces its impact
items.what: A random error is an unpredictable variation in measurements that causes readings to be higher or lower than expected by varying amounts. Random errors arise from uncontrolled variables and affect precision.
items.why: Because random errors are equally likely to cause results that are too high or too low, taking the mean of multiple trials reduces their overall impact. This is why repeatability (multiple trials) improves the reliability of results.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, variations in the exact volume of solutions pipetted each trial, or slight differences in reading the colour of glucose test strips, are random errors. Taking the average of three trials (0.00, 0.00, 0.00 → mean 0.00; then 10.0, 6.50, 6.50 → mean 7.70) reduces the influence of these random variations.

subtopic.name: Errors, Accuracy and Precision
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of experimental error — random and systematic — as well as the concepts of accuracy, precision, outliers and how to identify areas for improvement in investigation design.
subtopic.why: Understanding error analysis is essential for evaluating the quality of experimental results. VCE extended response tasks frequently require students to identify specific errors, explain their effect and propose improvements.

items.title: I can identify outliers in a dataset and explain how they should be handled
items.what: An outlier is a data value that is substantially different from the other values recorded for the same measurement. If time permits, the measurement should be repeated. If not, the outlier should be recorded in the table but excluded from the mean calculation.
items.why: Including outliers in a mean calculation distorts the average and reduces the reliability of the results. However, outliers must still be recorded to maintain an accurate and transparent logbook.
items.example: In a potato disc osmosis experiment, a mass reading of 3.31 g in a set of values around 2.00–2.13 g is an outlier. It should be recorded in the table but not included when calculating the mean for that trial set.

subtopic.name: Errors, Accuracy and Precision
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of experimental error — random and systematic — as well as the concepts of accuracy, precision, outliers and how to identify areas for improvement in investigation design.
subtopic.why: Understanding error analysis is essential for evaluating the quality of experimental results. VCE extended response tasks frequently require students to identify specific errors, explain their effect and propose improvements.

items.title: I can suggest evidence-based improvements to an investigation design
items.what: Identifying areas for improvement means suggesting specific changes to the method or equipment that would reduce identified errors, increase precision or accuracy, or improve validity. Improvements should address experimental design issues, not human mistakes.
items.why: VCE discussion sections require students to go beyond listing errors and propose meaningful, specific improvements. Suggestions should be directly linked to identified limitations in the investigation.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, the glucose test strips only have five reference colours. An improvement would be to replace them with a calibrated glucometer, which provides numerical readings to two decimal places, significantly increasing the precision of glucose concentration measurements.

subtopic.name: Errors, Accuracy and Precision
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of experimental error — random and systematic — as well as the concepts of accuracy, precision, outliers and how to identify areas for improvement in investigation design.
subtopic.why: Understanding error analysis is essential for evaluating the quality of experimental results. VCE extended response tasks frequently require students to identify specific errors, explain their effect and propose improvements.

items.title: I can describe the structure and key sections of a scientific poster
items.what: A VCE scientific poster includes the following sections in order: title, student name, introduction (including aim and hypothesis), methodology and methods, results, communication statement, discussion, conclusion, and references and acknowledgements.
items.why: The poster template is specified in the VCAA Chemistry Study Design. Students must follow this structure for School-assessed Coursework. The communication statement — a single engaging sentence summarising the key finding — occupies approximately one quarter of the poster.
items.example: A communication statement for the invertase investigation might read: 'The presence of the enzyme invertase increased the rate of glucose production from the hydrolysis of sucrose by a factor of six compared with the uninhibited reaction.' This is a single sentence and would be presented prominently on the poster.

subtopic.name: Scientific Communication
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the conventions of scientific communication for VCE Chemistry, including the structure and content of a scientific poster, the use of correct units and significant figures, referencing in Harvard format, and how to write a justified conclusion.
subtopic.why: The VCE Chemistry School-assessed Coursework requires students to present their investigation as a scientific poster of no more than 600 words. Mastery of these communication conventions is directly assessed and reflects skills used by professional scientists.

items.title: I can use correct SI units and convert between units used in chemistry
items.what: Quantitative results must be reported with appropriate SI units. Common conversions include: mL to L (divide by 1000), g to kg (divide by 1000), and concentration in mol L^-1 to g L^-1 (multiply by molar mass).
items.why: Incorrect or missing units in calculations and results tables cost marks in VCE assessments. Unit conversions are required for gas law calculations and mole calculations, making this a high-frequency skill.
items.example: To convert 250 mL to litres: 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 L. To convert a concentration of 0.500 mol L^-1 NaOH to g L^-1: 0.500 mol L^-1 × 40.00 g mol^-1 = 20.0 g L^-1.

items.title: I can determine the correct number of significant figures in a value
items.what: Significant figures indicate the precision of a measurement. All non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. Leading zeros are not significant. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant.
items.why: Reporting answers to an inappropriate number of significant figures is penalised in VCE. The number of significant figures in an answer should reflect the precision of the least precise measurement used in the calculation.
items.example: 34.980 has 5 significant figures (all digits including trailing zero after decimal). 10.0 has 3 significant figures (the trailing zero after the decimal is significant). 0.0034 has 2 significant figures (leading zeros are not significant, only the 3 and 4 are).

items.title: I can write a justified conclusion that evaluates evidence against a hypothesis
items.what: A conclusion briefly states the key finding of the investigation with reference to specific data, assesses whether the results support or do not support the hypothesis, and avoids introducing new information not discussed in the results and discussion. Terms such as 'supported' and 'indicated' are used rather than 'proved' or 'disproved'.
items.why: A conclusion is not simply a restatement of results. It must make a claim about what the data means in relation to the hypothesis and the broader chemistry. Using 'proved' implies absolute certainty, which is not appropriate for a single investigation.
items.example: Correct conclusion language: 'The results indicate that the presence of invertase increased the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose, with glucose concentration reaching 20.0 mg mL^-1 at 180 s compared with 3.00 mg mL^-1 in the absence of invertase. These results support the hypothesis.'

items.title: I can reference a source correctly using Harvard format
items.what: Harvard referencing requires four elements for most sources: author surname and initials, year of publication in brackets, title, and source details. References are listed in alphabetical order by author surname. Websites must include the URL and the date accessed.
items.why: Correct referencing is required in the poster to avoid plagiarism and to allow readers to locate the original sources. VCE assessment rubrics include marks for correct referencing format.
items.example: Book reference: Drummond, B., Maaser, S., Angley, L., Greaves, R., Fraser, S., Lucas, T., and Wang, Z. (2023). Cambridge Chemistry VCE Units 1 and 2. Cambridge University Press. items.title: I can interpret investigation outcomes in terms of broader chemical concepts
items.what: Interpreting outcomes means connecting the results of the investigation to the underlying chemical theory — for example, explaining how collision theory accounts for observed rate changes, or how enzyme mechanism explains the plateau in product concentration.
items.why: Results without chemical explanation demonstrate data recording but not scientific understanding. VCE rubrics reward students who can link experimental observations to relevant chemical models and theories.
items.example: In the invertase investigation, if glucose concentration plateaus at 20.0 mg mL^-1 after 180 s, a student can interpret this by noting that the substrate (sucrose) has been fully consumed, so no further hydrolysis can occur regardless of invertase concentration remaining.
